rows.question: What is the notice period before filing a cheque bounce complaint?
queries: What is the notice period before filing a cheque bounce complaint?
dishonour of cheque notice to drawer within thirty days of receipt of information
Negotiable Instruments Act section 138 notice demand payment
Negotiable Instruments Act section 142 limitation period for filing complaint
rows.answer:
- Where a cheque is returned unpaid by the bank, the payee or holder in due course must make a demand for payment by giving a notice in writing to the drawer within thirty days of receiving information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid, and the drawer must be given a period of fifteen days from the receipt of the notice to make the payment before a complaint can be filed [1][12].

Conditions and time limits:
- Validity period: The cheque must be presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier, as stated in Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1].
- Notice period: The written demand notice must be given to the drawer within thirty days of the receipt of information by the payee or holder in due course from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid, pursuant to Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1].
- Payment period: The drawer has fifteen days from the date of receipt of the notice to make the payment, according to Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1].

rows.question: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
queries: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
presumption as to consideration for negotiable instrument evidence
Negotiable Instruments Act section 118 presumption as to consideration
rows.answer:
- It shall be presumed, until the contrary is proved, that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration, under Section 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1].
- In the case of *K.P.O. Moideenkutty Hajee versus Pappu Manjooran and Anr.*, it is noted that Section 118(a) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 imposes a duty on the court to raise a presumption in favour of the plaintiff that the promissory note was made for consideration, which throws the burden of proof of failure of consideration on the maker [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 43 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, which covers a "Negotiable instrument made, etc., without consideration" and states that it creates no obligation of payment between the parties [2].
- Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, which covers "Presumption in favour of holder" and states that the holder of a cheque received it for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability [4].

rows.question: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?
queries: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?
contract voidable at option of party whose consent was caused by coercion fraud misrepresentation
Indian Contract Act section 19 voidability of agreements without free consent
Indian Contract Act section 15 coercion defined and section 18 misrepresentation defined
rows.answer: A contract can be avoided when consent to the agreement is caused by coercion or misrepresentation, making it a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused under Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. However, under the exception to Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a contract caused by misrepresentation or by fraudulent silence is not voidable if the party whose consent was so caused had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence [1]. Furthermore, an explanation to Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 states that a misrepresentation which did not cause the consent to a contract of the party to whom it was made does not render a contract voidable [1]. Under Section 15 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, coercion is defined as committing or threatening to commit any act forbidden by the Indian Penal Code, or the unlawful detaining or threatening to detain any property, to the prejudice of any person, with the intention of causing any person to enter into an agreement [2]. rows.question: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
queries: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
competency to contract age of majority soundness of mind disqualified by law
Indian Contract Act section 11
capacity of parties to contract unsound mind minor
topSources: The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 sO32
rows.answer: Every person is competent to enter into a contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which they are subject, who is of sound mind, and who is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which they are subject, as stated in Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1][12].

rows.question: What is the punishment for murder?
queries: What is the punishment for murder?
punishment for murder causing death of person culpable homicide
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita section 103 punishment for murder
Indian Penal Code section 302 punishment for murder
topSources: The Indian Penal Code, 45 of 1860 (Rep., Act 45 of 2023) s302
rows.answer:
Whoever commits murder is punished with death or imprisonment for life, and is also liable to fine, according to Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1]. 

When a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on the ground of race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground, each member of such group is punished with death or with imprisonment for life, and is also liable to fine under Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1]. 

Additionally, Section 104 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 states that whoever, being under sentence of imprisonment for life, commits murder, shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, which shall mean the remainder of that person's natural life [3].

In the Supreme Court judgment Bharatkumar Rameshchandra Barot versus State of Gujarat, the Supreme Court upheld the modification of a sentence to life imprisonment under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 [2].

- For a second or subsequent conviction under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the punishment is rigorous imprisonment for a term of not less than one year and up to five years, along with a fine [1].
- In cases of theft where the value of the stolen property is less than five thousand rupees and the person is convicted for the first time, upon returning the value of the property or restoring the stolen property, the punishment shall be community service under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1].

- Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 provides that whoever prints or engraves any matter, knowing or having good reason to believe that such matter is defamatory, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term up to two years, or with fine, or with both [1].

rows.question: When can a person accused of a non-bailable offence be released on bail?
queries: When can a person accused of a non-bailable offence be released on bail?

Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita section 480 bail in case of non-bailable offence

topSources: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s480
The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 s437
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s482
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s2
rows.answer:
A person accused of a non-bailable offence may be released on bail by a police officer in charge of a station or by a Court other than the High Court or Court of Session, unless there appear reasonable grounds for believing that the person has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, or is a previously convicted person as specified by law [1][2][4][9][11][12]. 

A Court or police officer may also release an accused on bail at any stage of the investigation, inquiry, or trial if it appears that there are no reasonable grounds for believing the accused committed a non-bailable offence, but there are sufficient grounds for further inquiry into guilt [1][2][4][9][12]. 

Conditions and time limits:
- If the accused is a child, a woman, sick, or infirm, the Court may direct release on bail even in cases punishable with death or imprisonment for life or involving previous convictions [1][2][4].
- If the Court is satisfied that it is just and proper for any other special reason, it may direct the release of a previously convicted person [1][2][4].

rows.answer: An arbitral award may be set aside by the Court only if the party making the application establishes on the basis of the record of the arbitral tribunal that a party was under some incapacity, the arbitration agreement is not valid under the applicable law, the party was not given proper notice of the appointment of an arbitrator or of the arbitral proceedings or was otherwise unable to present its case, the award deals with a dispute not contemplated by or not falling within the terms of the submission to arbitration or contains decisions on matters beyond the scope of submission, or the composition of the arbitral tribunal or arbitral procedure was not in accordance with the agreement of the parties or Part I of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 [1]. In addition, the Court may set aside an award if it finds that the subject-matter of the dispute is not capable of settlement by arbitration under the law for the time being in force, or the arbitral award is in conflict with the public policy of India [1]. rows.question: How is a sale of immovable property defined and completed?
queries: How is a sale of immovable property defined and completed?

rows.answer:
Under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a sale is defined as a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised or part-paid and part-promised [1]. According to the Supreme Court judgment in Lucknow Nagar Nigam & Others versus Kohli Brothers Colour Lab. Pvt. Ltd. & Others, a sale constitutes a transfer of ownership from one person to another, meaning all rights and interests possessed in the property are transferred with free consent for a price called consideration, and title passes from the seller to the buyer only when the conveyance is regarded in accordance with law without the transferor retaining any part of their interest or right [11].

For how a sale is made:
- For tangible immovable property valued at one hundred rupees and upwards, or for a reversion or other intangible thing, a sale can be made only by a registered instrument under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [1]. rows.question: What are the inherent powers of a civil court?
queries: What are the inherent powers of a civil court?
inherent powers of court civil court saving of inherent powers
Code of Civil Procedure section 151
Code of Civil Procedure order rule inherent jurisdiction
topSources: The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 s151
The Metro Railways (Construction of Works) Act, 1978 s16B
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s528
The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 s11
The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 sO15AR6
rows.answer:
I couldn't find a direct definition of the inherent powers of a civil court in the Acts I searched. 

However, Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 states that nothing in the Code shall be deemed to limit or otherwise affect the inherent power of the Court to make such orders as may be necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of the process of the Court [1]. Additionally, Section 16B of the Metro Railways (Construction of Works) Act, 1978 provides that the competent authority and the appellate authority may exercise powers of the nature referred to in section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 to the same extent and for the same purposes as such powers are exercisable by civil courts [2]. 

Regarding relevant Supreme Court judgments, the excerpt from "State of Maharashtra versus Maharau Srawan Hatkar" notes that while Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 gives inherent power to the Court, it is intended only to prevent abuse of the process of the court or to meet the ends of justice [1]. Only Supreme Court judgments are searched as short excerpts, and High Court and tribunal decisions are not included yet.

rows.question: What is theft punishment?
queries: What is theft punishment?
punishment for theft
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita section 303 theft punishment
Indian Penal Code section 379 punishment for theft
topSources: The Indian Penal Code, 45 of 1860 (Rep., Act 45 of 2023) s379
rows.answer:
Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both, and for a second or subsequent conviction, with rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than one year and up to five years, along with a fine, under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1]. For a first-time conviction where the stolen property's value is less than five thousand rupees, upon returning or restoring the stolen property, the punishment shall be community service under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 305 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 covers theft in a dwelling house, means of transportation, or place of worship, etc., with imprisonment up to seven years and a fine [7].
- Section 306 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 covers theft by a clerk or servant of property in possession of the master, with imprisonment up to seven years and a fine [5].
- Section 328 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 covers punishment for intentionally running vessel aground or ashore with intent to commit theft, etc., with imprisonment up to ten years and a fine [3].
